title: Why Absalom Burned Joab’s Field to Get Attention
paragraphs: Why Absalom Burned Joab’s Field to Get Attention
There are people reading this right now who never wanted to become destructive.
You did not wake up one morning hoping to become bitter. You did not plan to become angry. You did not want your pain to start spilling onto innocent people.
But ignored wounds eventually become dangerous fires.
That is the terrifying tension hidden inside one of the Bible’s most emotionally explosive moments.
A prince. A father who stopped speaking to him. A commander who ignored him. A broken son screaming for someone to finally look at him.
And suddenly… fields are burning.
Most people know Absalom as the rebellious son who tried to steal King David’s throne. But before Absalom became dangerous publicly… he was dying internally.
And one of the clearest cries for attention in all of Scripture came through smoke.
The story is found in 2 Samuel 14.
Absalom had spent years emotionally isolated.
After murdering his brother Amnon for violating Tamar, Absalom fled into exile for three years. Eventually Joab convinced King David to allow Absalom to return to Jerusalem.
But there was a brutal condition attached.
David refused to see his own son.
Imagine living in the same city as your father while being treated like you no longer exist.
The Hebrew language in 2 Samuel 14 carries emotional weight many readers never fully notice.
When Scripture says David would not see Absalom’s face, the Hebrew reads:
"וּפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ לֹא רָאָה"
Transliterated: “U’penei ha’melekh lo ra’ah.”
Literal sense: “He did not see the face of the king.”
In ancient Hebrew culture, seeing someone’s face represented restored relationship, acceptance, reconciliation, and covenant peace.
This was not merely physical distance.
This was relational rejection.
Absalom was home… but emotionally fatherless.
And some people understand that kind of pain too well.
You can live in the same house with someone and still feel abandoned.
You can sleep beside someone and still feel invisible.
You can sit in church every Sunday and still feel spiritually unseen.
Absalom spent two full years in Jerusalem without seeing David.
Two years.
Silence changes people.
Ignored pain mutates.
Unaddressed wounds evolve.
And eventually Absalom reached a breaking point.
Scripture says he repeatedly called for Joab.
Joab ignored him.
Again. And again. And again.
Then comes one of the most cinematic moments in the entire Old Testament.
2 Samuel 14:30:
“Therefore he said unto his servants, See, Joab’s field is near mine, and he hath barley there; go and set it on fire.”
The Hebrew phrase for “set it on fire” is:
"וְהַצִּיתוּהָ בָאֵשׁ"
Transliteration: “Ve’hatzituha ba’esh.”
Literal meaning: “Consume it with fire.”
This was not accidental.
This was intentional destruction born from emotional desperation.
And suddenly Joab came running.
The same man who ignored Absalom repeatedly immediately showed up when his field started burning.
That detail is devastating.
Because Absalom learned something many wounded people quietly learn:
Sometimes destruction gets attention faster than honesty.

That is why some people explode. That is why some people sabotage relationships. That is why some people self-destruct publicly. That is why some people become toxic. That is why some people lash out online. That is why some people destroy the very people they love.
Not always because they are evil.
Sometimes because pain convinced them fire is the only language people respond to.
And before judging Absalom too quickly… some of us have done similar things emotionally.
Maybe not with literal fire.
But with words. With manipulation. With cold silence. With rage. With rebellion. With reckless decisions. With hidden addictions. With spiritual compromise.
Sometimes people burn things because they are screaming internally:
“Will somebody finally notice me?”
This story becomes even heavier when we understand Joab.
Joab was not merely a military commander.
He was the bridge between Absalom and David.
Absalom believed Joab had the power to restore connection.
But Joab stopped responding.
And neglected people often become emotionally unpredictable.
The tragedy is that Absalom never truly healed.
He learned how to gain attention.
But he never learned surrender.
There is a massive difference.
Attention can temporarily soothe pain. Only God can transform it.
That is why wounded people who receive visibility without healing often become more dangerous, not less.
Absalom eventually became obsessed with image, power, admiration, and control.
2 Samuel 14:25 says:
“Now in all Israel there was none to be so much praised as Absalom for his beauty.”
The Hebrew word for beauty here is:
"יָפֶה"
“Yafeh.”
Meaning: Beautiful, attractive, pleasing, externally admirable.
Absalom mastered external appearance while internally decaying.
And that is still happening today.
Some people look successful publicly while bleeding privately.
Some social media smiles are covering emotional funerals.
Some loud personalities are hiding abandoned hearts.
Some rebellious behavior is actually unresolved grief wearing armor.
This is why Jesus did not merely address behavior.
He addressed hearts.
Religion often focuses on visible flames. Jesus investigates hidden wounds.
The Gospel reveals something extraordinary.
God does not wait for us to burn fields before responding.
One of the greatest differences between earthly relationships and Christ is this:
Jesus moves toward broken people before they self-destruct completely.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
The Greek phrase for “commendeth his love” is:
"συνίστησιν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀγάπην"
Transliteration: “Synistēsin tēn heautou agapēn.”
Meaning: God demonstrates, proves, establishes His own sacrificial love.
Not after perfection. Not after cleanup. Not after image management.
While we were still broken.
That changes everything.
Absalom had to create fire to get attention.
Jesus climbed onto a cross because Heaven already saw us.
And maybe that is the part somebody desperately needed to hear today.
You do not need to destroy yourself to be seen by God.
You do not need to perform pain for Heaven to notice you.
You do not need to become louder, darker, angrier, or more reckless for Jesus to care.
He already sees you.
The Hebrew concept of God “seeing” carries deep covenant intimacy.
In Genesis 16:13 Hagar calls God:
"אֵל רֳאִי"
“El Roi.”
Meaning: “The God who sees me.”
Not the God who merely watches.
The God who truly sees.
Your hidden exhaustion. Your disappointment. Your private grief. Your secret shame. Your fear. Your loneliness. Your resentment. Your confusion.
Some people reading this have spent years silently asking:
“Does anybody notice what I’m carrying?”
God does.
But there is another warning inside Absalom’s story that cannot be ignored.
Pain that is not surrendered to God eventually starts spreading.
Absalom’s unresolved wounds eventually divided an entire kingdom.
Hurt people often hurt people.
Not because pain excuses sin. But because untreated wounds become spiritual infection.
This is why forgiveness matters. This is why repentance matters. This is why healing matters. This is why humility matters.
Some people are one ignored wound away from becoming someone they never imagined.
And that is why we desperately need Christ.
Not motivational spirituality. Not image-based religion. Not church performance.
We need heart resurrection.
The Gospel is not behavior modification.
It is supernatural transformation.
Ezekiel 36:26 says:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.”
The Hebrew phrase:
"לֵב חָדָשׁ"
“Lev chadash.”
A new heart.
Not patched. Not cosmetically improved. Not temporarily distracted.
Made new.
There are people trying to heal eternal wounds with temporary attention.
It will never be enough.
More validation will not save you. More followers will not save you. More money will not save you. More applause will not save you. More distractions will not save you.
Only Jesus can reach the places pain buried alive.
And perhaps the saddest part of Absalom’s story is this:
The son who desperately wanted connection eventually died hanging from a tree.
Suspended between heaven and earth.
Broken by pride. Consumed by rebellion. Destroyed by unresolved pain.
David wept bitterly afterward.
2 Samuel 18:33:
“O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee.”
One of the most heartbreaking cries in Scripture.
But unlike David… Jesus actually did die for us.
That is the Gospel.
Christ took the punishment rebellion deserved.
The Son of God stepped into the destruction human sin created.
And through the cross, broken sons and daughters can finally come home.
No more pretending. No more performing. No more burning fields to feel visible.
Grace sees you already.
And maybe this article exposed something hidden inside you.

Maybe you have been acting strong while quietly bleeding. Maybe your anger is actually grief. Maybe your rebellion is rooted in rejection. Maybe your exhaustion comes from carrying wounds nobody noticed.
Jesus is still calling you toward healing.
Not condemnation. Healing.
Your honesty might help someone else finally stop suffering silently.
Some wounds do not scream through tears. Sometimes they scream through fire.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Sinunog ni Absalom ang Bukirin ni Joab Para Lang Mapansin
May mga taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na hindi naman talaga gustong maging mapanira.
Hindi mo pinangarap maging galit. Hindi mo hiniling na maging malamig ang puso mo. Hindi mo gustong dumating sa puntong ang sugat mo ay nagsisimulang makasakit ng ibang tao.
Pero ang sakit na hindi pinapansin… kalaunan nagiging apoy.
At iyon ang isa sa pinakamabigat na emosyonal na eksena sa buong Biblia.
Isang prinsipe. Isang amang tumigil nang kausapin siya. Isang lalaking paulit-ulit siyang binale-wala. Isang sugatang anak na desperadong gustong mapansin.
At biglang… may nasusunog na bukirin.
Kilala ng marami si Absalom bilang rebeldeng anak ni David na nagtangkang agawin ang trono. Pero bago naging mapanganib si Absalom sa publiko… matagal muna siyang namatay sa loob.
At isa sa pinakamalalakas na sigaw para mapansin sa buong Kasulatan ay dumaan sa apoy.
Matatagpuan ang kuwento sa 2 Samuel 14.

Matapos patayin ni Absalom ang kapatid niyang si Amnon dahil sa ginawa nito kay Tamar, tumakas siya at namuhay sa pagkakatapon nang tatlong taon. Kalaunan, nakumbinsi ni Joab si Haring David na payagang makabalik si Absalom sa Jerusalem.
Pero may mabigat na kondisyon.
Ayaw siyang makita ng sarili niyang ama.
Isipin mong nasa iisang siyudad lang kayo ng ama mo… pero para kang hindi umiiral.
Sa Hebrew, nang sabihin ng Kasulatan na hindi nakita ni Absalom ang mukha ng hari, ito ang nakasulat:
"וּפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ לֹא רָאָה"
Transliteration: “U’penei ha’melekh lo ra’ah.”
Literal na kahulugan: “Hindi niya nakita ang mukha ng hari.”
Sa kulturang Hebreo, ang “makita ang mukha” ay simbolo ng pagtanggap, pagkakasundo, at muling pagpapanumbalik ng relasyon.
Hindi lang ito simpleng distansya.
Ito ay emosyonal na pagtanggi.
Nasa bahay si Absalom… pero parang ulila pa rin.
At may mga taong nakakaramdam niyan hanggang ngayon.
Pwede kayong nasa iisang bahay… pero pakiramdam mo mag-isa ka.
Pwede kayong magkatabi sa kama… pero hindi ka na nakikita.
Pwede kang magsimba linggo-linggo… pero parang walang nakakakita sa totoong dinadala mo.
Dalawang taon nanatili si Absalom sa Jerusalem nang hindi man lang nakikita si David.
Dalawang taon.
Binabago ng katahimikan ang tao.
Kapag hindi ginagamot ang sugat… lumalala.
Kapag hindi inaayos ang sakit… kumakalat.
At dumating si Absalom sa sukdulan.
Paulit-ulit niyang ipinatawag si Joab.
Pero hindi siya pinansin.
Paulit-ulit.
Hanggang dumating ang isa sa pinaka-cinematic na tagpo sa Lumang Tipan.
2 Samuel 14:30:
“Kaya sinabi niya sa kaniyang mga alipin, Tingnan ninyo, ang bukid ni Joab ay malapit sa akin, at mayroon siyang sebada roon; puntahan ninyo at sunugin ninyo.”
Sa Hebrew, ang “sunugin” ay:
"וְהַצִּיתוּהָ בָאֵשׁ"
Transliteration: “Ve’hatzituha ba’esh.”
Literal na kahulugan: “Silaban ninyo ng apoy.”
Hindi ito aksidente.
Sinadya ito.
Desperadong sigaw ito ng isang pusong hindi na matiis na hindi mapansin.
At biglang dumating si Joab.
Ang lalaking paulit-ulit siyang hindi pinapansin… agad sumipot nang may nasusunog na.
Napakabigat ng detalye na iyon.
Dahil may mga sugatang tao ring natututong ganito:
“Minsan, mas mabilis mapansin ang gulo kaysa katotohanan.”

Kaya may mga taong sumasabog. Kaya may mga relasyon na sinisira. Kaya may mga taong unti-unting winawasak ang sarili nila. Kaya may mga taong nagiging toxic. Kaya may mga taong nagrerebelde. Kaya may mga taong lumalayo sa Diyos.
Hindi palaging dahil masama sila.
Minsan dahil naniwala silang ang apoy lang ang wikang pinapakinggan ng mundo.
At bago mo husgahan si Absalom… baka may mga pagkakataon ding parang ganoon tayo.
Hindi man literal na apoy.
Pero sa masasakit na salita. Sa galit. Sa pananahimik. Sa paglayo. Sa pagtatago. Sa bisyo. Sa kasalanan. Sa panlalamig.
May mga taong naninira dahil may sumisigaw sa loob nila:
“May makakapansin ba sa akin?”
Mas mabigat pa ang kuwento kapag naunawaan natin kung sino si Joab.
Hindi lang siya sundalo.
Siya ang tulay ni Absalom pabalik kay David.
At nang tumigil siyang sumagot… lalong naging magulo si Absalom.
Kapag matagal pinababayaan ang sugat… nagiging mapanganib ang puso.
Pero ang tunay na trahedya ay ito:
Natuto si Absalom kung paano kumuha ng atensyon.
Pero hindi siya natutong magpagaling.
Magkaibang bagay iyon.
Kayang pansamantalang patahimikin ng atensyon ang sakit. Pero Diyos lang ang kayang magbago ng puso.
Kaya maraming sugatang tao na kapag sumikat… lalo pang nasisira.
Kalaunan, naging obsessed si Absalom sa itsura, kapangyarihan, at paghanga ng tao.
2 Samuel 14:25:
“Sa buong Israel ay walang lalaking pinupuri nang higit kay Absalom dahil sa kaniyang kagandahan.”
Ang salitang Hebrew para sa “kagandahan” ay:
"יָפֶה"
“Yafeh.”
Ibig sabihin: Maganda, kaaya-aya, kahanga-hanga sa panlabas.
Napaganda ni Absalom ang panlabas niyang anyo habang unti-unting nasisira ang loob niya.
At nangyayari pa rin iyon hanggang ngayon.
May mga mukhang masaya online… pero umiiyak kapag mag-isa.
May mga mukhang matatag… pero wasak na pala sa loob.
May mga taong maingay… dahil takot silang marinig ang katahimikan.
Ito ang dahilan kung bakit hindi lang ugali ang tinitingnan ni Jesus.
Puso ang hinahanap Niya.
Madalas ang relihiyon nakatuon sa nakikitang apoy. Pero si Cristo… diretso sa sugat.
At dito lalong gumaganda ang Ebanghelyo.
Hindi hinihintay ng Diyos na sirain muna natin ang lahat bago Niya tayo lapitan.
Romans 5:8:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Sa Greek:
"συνίστησιν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀγάπην"
Transliteration: “Synistēsin tēn heautou agapēn.”
Kahulugan: Ipinapakita at pinatutunayan ng Diyos ang Kaniyang pag-ibig.
Hindi pagkatapos nating maging malinis. Hindi pagkatapos nating magbago. Hindi pagkatapos nating ayusin ang sarili.
Habang makasalanan pa tayo.
Habang sugatan pa tayo.
Habang magulo pa tayo.
Hindi kailangang magsunog ng bukirin para mapansin ng Diyos.
Nakikita ka na Niya noon pa.
Sa Genesis 16:13, tinawag ni Hagar ang Diyos na:
"אֵל רֳאִי"
“El Roi.”
Ang ibig sabihin: “Ang Diyos na nakakakita sa akin.”
Hindi lang basta nanonood.
Kundi tunay na nakakakita.
Nakikita Niya ang pagod mo. Nakikita Niya ang lihim mong iyak. Nakikita Niya ang sugat na tinatago mo. Nakikita Niya ang bigat na hindi mo masabi. Nakikita Niya ang galit na hindi mo maintindihan.
At baka may nagbabasa nito na matagal nang nagtatanong:
“May nakakapansin pa ba sa akin?”
Oo.
Nakikita ka ng Diyos.
Pero may babala rin sa kuwento ni Absalom.
Ang sakit na hindi isinusuko sa Diyos… kalaunan nakakasakit din ng iba.
Ang sugat ni Absalom ay hindi lang sumira sa kaniya.
Hinati nito ang buong kaharian.
Kaya mahalaga ang pagpapatawad. Kaya mahalaga ang pagsisisi. Kaya mahalaga ang pagpapagaling. Kaya mahalaga ang pagpapakumbaba.
May mga taong isang sugat na lang ang layo bago maging taong hindi nila akalaing magiging sila.
At iyan ang dahilan kung bakit kailangan natin si Cristo.
Hindi lang religion. Hindi lang church attendance. Hindi lang magandang imahe.
Kailangan natin ng bagong puso.
Ezekiel 36:26:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.”
Sa Hebrew:
"לֵב חָדָשׁ"
“Lev chadash.”
Bagong puso.
Hindi patched. Hindi tinakpan lang. Hindi dinistract lang.
Bagong-bago.
Maraming tao ang sinusubukang pagalingin ang eternal na sugat gamit ang temporaryong atensyon.
Pero hindi iyon sapat.
Hindi followers ang makakapagligtas. Hindi validation. Hindi pera. Hindi kasikatan. Hindi applause.
Si Jesus lang.
At marahil ang pinakamalungkot sa kuwento ni Absalom ay ito:
Ang anak na desperadong gustong mapalapit… namatay na nakabitin sa puno.
Wasak ng pride. Nilamon ng rebelyon. Sinira ng sugat na hindi gumaling.
At umiyak si David.
2 Samuel 18:33:
“O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee.”
Isa sa pinakamasakit na iyak sa buong Biblia.
Pero hindi tulad ni David… talagang namatay si Jesus para sa atin.
Iyan ang Ebanghelyo.
Pinasan ni Cristo ang parusang dapat sana ay atin.
Para ang mga sugatang anak ay makauwi na sa wakas.
Wala nang pagtatago. Wala nang pagpapanggap. Wala nang pagsusunog para lang mapansin.
Nakikita ka na ng biyaya.
At baka may tinamaan talaga sa puso mo habang binabasa ito.
Baka matagal ka nang pagod. Baka ang galit mo ay sugat lang pala. Baka ang pagrerebelde mo ay bunga ng rejection. Baka tahimik ka lang… pero unti-unti ka nang nasusunog sa loob.
Hindi ka pa tinatalikuran ni Jesus.
Tinatawag ka pa rin Niya papunta sa kagalingan.
Kung tumama ito sa puso mo, huwag mo lang basta i-scroll.
At maging totoo ka sa comments.
Baka ang honesty mo ang makatulong para may ibang taong hindi na magdusa nang tahimik.
May mga sugat na hindi sumisigaw sa pamamagitan ng luha. Minsan… apoy ang ginagamit nila.
